Regioselective 1,4-/1,3-Difunctionalization of 1,3-Enynes with
Selenosulfonates in Water
Hong-He Deng, Shi-Yin Tian, Jia-Hui Han, Xin-Yu Liu, Weidong Rao, Shu-Su Shen, Daopeng Sheng,
Zhao-Ying Yang, and Shun-Yi Wang*

ABSTRACT: 1,4-/1,3-Regioselective bifunctionalization of 1,3-
enynes with selenosulfonates in water under catalyst-free
conditions for the construction of sulfonyl allene and 1,3-
disulfonyl-conjugated dienes respectively have been developed.
The reactions feature mild reaction conditions in aqueous solution
and remarkable regioselectivity controlled by substrates.
1. INTRODUCTION
Sulfur-containing compounds are widely found in natural
products, pharmaceutical molecules, and functional materials,
so their synthesis has attracted much attention.
1
Also, sulfur-
containing molecules can serve as important intermediates and
ligands for organic synthesis.
2
Selenium (Se), as an important
biological trace element, plays a vital role in humans and other
higher animals.
3
Allenes are an important component of
organic chemistry with a unique cumulative structure.
4
In
recent years, the unique structure and properties of allenes
have attracted more and more scientists to study them, and the
synthesis of allene derivatives has received extensive attention
and a variety of synthetic methods have been established.
5
Most of the current methods for constructing allene
compounds are to first generate allene radical positive or
negative intermediates and then further transform them, but
there are relatively few methods for constructing allene
compounds based on allene radical intermediates.
6
As a
specialized structure in which olefins and alkynes are directly
linked, 1,3-enynes have high reactivity and a large number of
reactive sites. 1,3-Enynes have been developed as versatile
structural units to obtain a variety of highly useful molecular
architectures,
7
including alkyne-propyl compounds,
8
biphen-
yls,
9
and dienes.
10
Based on the specificity of the 1,3-enyne-
containing skeleton and our group’s research on sulfur and
selenium compounds, we envisioned whether we could cleverly
design compounds containing the 1,3-enyne skeleton and
sulfur and selenium-containing
11
elements to synthesize the
connecting skeleton.
Based on the literature research, we found that most of the
methods for the construction of allene compounds by 1,3-
enynes require the use of metal catalysis. With the further
investigation of the allene chemistry and the development of
the concept of green chemistry, metal-free catalytic methods
for the construction of allene compounds have been
developed. In 2019, Ma’s
12
group reported a copper-catalyzed
1,4-addition reaction of sulfonyl iodides with 1,3-enynes
affording various allenyl halides in high yields under mild
conditions has been developed. In the same year, Wang’s
13
group reported a nickel catalyst to generate different
fluoroalkyl radicals from readily available and structurally
diverse fluoroalkyl halides to access 1,4-difunctionalization of
1,3-enynes by a radical relay. In 2020, Bao’s
14
group reported
the reaction of 1,3-enyne with NFSI for the construction of
difluoromethylated allene compounds (Scheme, 1). In 2021,
Du’s
15
group reported the NHC-catalyzed 1,4-alkylcarbonyla-
tion of 1,3-enynes, which introduced difluoromethyl in the
alkyne backbone without metal catalysis (Scheme, 1). This
method is applicable to a range of alkyl radical precursors and
has good regioselectivity and functional group tolerance. In
contrast, our group reported a metal-free catalytic selective
bifunctionalization reaction of 1,3-enynes with selenosulfonate.
Both 1,4-bifunctionalization of 1,3-enynes to construct allene
compounds and 1,3-bifunctionalization of 1,3-enynes to
construct disulfonyl-conjugated dienes can be achieved by
modulation of the substrate.

2. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
Initially, as envisioned, we stirred 1,3-enyne (1a) with
selenosulfonate (2a) in DMSO solvent at room temperature
under nitrogen protection using copper catalysis for 12 h.
However, the target product (3a) was isolated in only 12%
yield. (Table 1, entry 1). Encouraged by this promising result,
we performed a series of conditional screens. When we added
K
3
PO
4
to the system, we found that the reaction was
completely inhibited (Table 1, entry 2). Next, we screened
the solvent types for the reaction and we found that both
methanol and water could be used as the optimal solvents with
an elevated yield of 27% (Table 1, entries 3−9). Considering
that temperature may have a facilitating effect on the reaction,
we explored the temperature of the reaction and found that the
best yield was obtained when the temperature was increased to
60 °C (Table 1, entries 10−12). On this basis, the yield was
further enhanced when we increased the amount of
selenosulfonate to 2 equiv (Table 1, entry 13). We tried to
add no ligand to the system and found that the yield decreased.
However, when both copper and ligand were not added, the
yield could still reach 50%, while reducing the amount of
selenosulfonate, the yield decreased slightly (Table 1, entries
14−16). Since both methanol and water were the optimal
solvents, we envisioned whether a mixture of solvents could be
used to further enhance the yield of this reaction. By adjusting
the ratio of the two solvents, we found that the yield could be
increased to 76% when the ratio of water to methanol was 9:1
(Table 1, entries 17−19).
With the optimized reaction conditions in hand, we explored
the substrate scope of 1,3-enynes (Scheme 2). It was found
that the substitution position of the methyl group on the
benzene ring can have a significant effect on the yields. When
the methyl group in the aromatic ring is located at the meta-
and para-positions, target products 3c and 3d were obtained in
moderate yields. When the aromatic ring with the methyl
group substituted at the ortho-position, the yield of target
product 3b is only 16% for the hindrance effect. The reactions
of para-ethyl, para-tert-butyl, and meta-methoxy substituted
substrates underwent smoothly to afford corresponding
products 3e−3g in moderate yields. It should be noted that
the reaction of biphenyl-based 1,3-enynes led to corresponding
product 3h in 73% yield. In addition, pyridines, thiophenes,
and halogen-substituted 1,3-enynes with heteroatoms all could
be applied to the reaction with 2a to yield desired products
3i−3l in moderate yields. The reaction of substrate bearing
trimethylsilyl group with 2a could also afford corresponding
product 3m in 30% yield. Unfortunately, the reaction failed
when the substrate bearing ester group and carboxylic acid as
well as cyclopropane.

Next, we investigated the substrate generalization of
selenosulfonates (Scheme 3). It was found that when alkyl-
substituted selenosulfonates were used, corresponding prod-
ucts 4a−4b could not be obtained. Using aryl-substituted
selenosulfonates, corresponding products 4c and 4d could be
obtained in good yields, for example, when selenosulfonates
containing methyl substitution at different positions were used
for the reaction, although the position of the substituent would
have an effect on the yields, with the adjacent substituted. The
reaction is better with adjacent substituted methyl groups than
with para-substituted methyl groups. When the reaction was
carried out using selenosulfonates containing the electron-
donating group methoxy substitution, corresponding product
4e could be obtained in 59% yield. when the reaction was
carried out using halogen-substituted selenosulfonates con-
taining electron-absorbing groups, corresponding products 4f
and 4g were obtained in 65% and 71% yields, respectively. In
addition, the selenosulfonates containing naphthalene rings
also gave corresponding product 4h in 70% yield. However,
the pyridine selenosulfonate containing heteroatoms could not
allow the reaction to take place.
To our surprise, in the process of substrate expansion,
pyridine-substituted 1,3-enynes afforded another product, 5a,
in 15% yield (Scheme 4), in addition to the production of
allene product 3i. On the basis of the template reaction
conditions, we then carried out optimization screening of the
reaction conditions (see SI Table S1). Finally, corresponding
product 5a could be obtained in 68% yield when H
2
O was
used as the solvent and the temperature was 80 °C.
Subsequently, under optimal conditions, we investigated the
functional group tolerance of the reaction (Scheme 5). We
found that for methyl with electron-donating effect corre-
sponding products 5b is obtained in lower yields. Sub-
sequently, the aryl ring of selenosulfonates with electron-
donating and electron-absorbing groups on the aromatic ring,
respectively, we found that the substrate with methoxy gives
target product 5c in only trace yield, while the halogen-
substituted and trifluoromethyl-substituted aryl selenosulfo-
nates give target products 5d−5f in moderate yields. It is
possible that the alkyl-substituted trifluoromethyl selenosulfo-
nate could not react smoothly due to a large site barrier. In
addition, the naphthalene ring-substituted selenosulfonate also
could not allow the reaction to proceed smoothly.
To investigate the feasibility of the reaction, we expanded
the reaction scale to 4 and 10 mmol and found that the yield of
the target product was 76% and 62%, respectively (Scheme
6).Then a series of controlled experiments were performed to
investigate the reaction mechanism. The reaction was
completely inhibited by adding TEMPO to the reaction
system under standard reaction conditions. The yield of 3a was
dramatically reduced to 15% by adding BHT (Scheme 6 a,b).
By replacing the selenosulfonate with a thiosulfonate or with
combination of thiosulfonate and diselenide, the reaction still
did not occur (Scheme 6 c,d). The pyridine-substituted 1,3-
enyne still did not react with the thiosulfonate, but the allene
product could be obtained with the thiosulfonate and
diselenide (Scheme 6 e,f). The reaction of 3i with 2a could
lead to allene disulfonated product 5a in 58% yield (Scheme 6
g).

Based on the relevant literatures and the controlled
experiments we performed, we propose a possible reaction
mechanism (Scheme 7). First, the selenosulfonate undergoes
homolytic cleavage under heating conditions to produce the
sulfone radical and the selenium radical. Next, the sulfone
radical attacks the olefin of 1,3-enynes to give the allyl radical
intermediate A. Allyl radical intermediate A undergoes
isomerization to give allene radical intermediate B, followed
by the capture of intermediate B by the selenium radical to
give product 3. When the substrate is a pyridine-substituted
1,3-enynes, the product is further isomerized to give
intermediate C. Then, the sulfone radical attacks the olefin
to generate intermediate D. Subsequently, D is trapped by the
solvent to give intermediate E. Following the retro-Micheal
reaction of E, 5 is observed.
3. CONCLUSION
In conclusion, we developed a metal-free/catalyst-free
regioselective 1,3/1,4-bifunctionalization reaction of 1,3-
enynes with selenosulfonate. By modulating the substrate,
both 1,4 bifunctionalization of 1,3-enynes and 1,3-bifunction-
alization of 1,3-enynes can be achieved to construct a allene
compound and a disulfonyl conjugated diene. The reaction
does not require metal catalysis, is simple to operate, uses a
green solvent, and provides a new idea for the construction of
allene compounds and conjugated dienes.
